te.title: Noisy pump since the feed tank was changed
te.sit: The tank farm switched the feed source to T200 yesterday. Pump A has become noisy and FRC-100 is slightly low with V100 opening.

te.title: The lazy twin is now B
te.sit: Pump A went back to the workshop last month and is now the spare; B is running. FRC-100 is short with its output at 100 %. The shift says "B must be the lazy one this time".

te.title: Short of feed, pump A gauge high

meta.title: Troubleshooting report — TE-1 The lazy twin (Parallel Pump Station P-200A/B)
meta.sit: Pump A is usually running; pump B, identical to A, is the spare. FRC-100 shows that not enough feed is going to the cat cracker although its output is at 100 %. Last week the operators switched from A to B and the flow came back. Pump B is scheduled for maintenance next week, so A must deliver. What is wrong?

0.1.unit: Two identical centrifugal pumps, P-200A and P-200B (3600 rpm, 10 kW, shut-off head A 45.0 m, B 46.5 m), sit in parallel between the common suction header (T200 → V200 → strainer S-200, local gauge PI-209) and a common discharge header. Each leg has a suction valve (V202 / V206), the pump, a local gauge between pump and check valve (PI-210 / PI-220), a check valve and a discharge valve (V201 / V205). The header feeds FE-100 and V100 (FRC-100, 14 L/s, the cat cracker’s set point), the steam preheater E-100 (60 → 150 °C, TV-110 in MAN) and the cat-cracker feed drum D-150. Normally A runs and B is the spare, lined up with V205 and V206 open.

rows.what: FRC-100 reads 11.22 L/s against its 14 L/s set point with the output at 100 %
Last week the operators changed over to B and the flow came back; now A is running again

0.4.ctx: Day shift, pump A running, B the spare lined up (V205 and V206 open). No maintenance or operating change reported today. B is due for maintenance next week, so A must carry the feed. Design values in the snapshot are the design point (A running, 14 L/s).

R.1.p: A centrifugal pump runs where its head curve ΔH = H0·s² − k·Q² meets the system curve (24 m static to D-150 plus the losses of the line, V100 and E-100). Two pumps in parallel share the suction and discharge headers, so each leg needs a check valve: when one pump is idle, its check valve must hold the header pressure off the idle casing. A local gauge between pump and check valve reads the casing: on a running pump the discharge head, on an idle pump with a tight check valve only the suction head. FRC-100 can only open V100; once V100 is at 100 % the flow is whatever the pumps and the system give. The motor current rises with the flow the pump makes.

R.2.eq: ΔH = H0·s² − k·Q² (pump);  H = 24 + K(x)·Q² (system);  Q_pump = Q_FE-100 + Q_lost

sym.m: Head the pump adds ≈ casing gauge (PI-210 / PI-220) − suction gauge PI-209
Shut-off head at 3600 rpm: A 45.0 m, B 46.5 m
Pump flow (off the curve) or the flow at FE-100 (FRC-100)
Line + V100 + E-100 resistance at V100 opening x

rows.info: Pump A is usually running; pump B, identical to A, is the spare. FRC-100 shows that not enough feed is going to the cat cracker although its output is at 100 %. Last week the operators switched from A to B and the flow came back. Pump B is scheduled for maintenance next week, so A must deliver. What is wrong?
“B is the good pump; A is tired — just run B until its maintenance.”
FRC-100 11.22 L/s, OUT 100 %, V100 100 %; FRC-100 LO standing since 00:00:01
D-150 44.3 → 33.2 % in 20 min; LI-150 LO at 30 % in about 11 min more

1.3.safn: No trip near: TI-212 60.1 °C (alarm 85, TSHH 110), II-210 14.2 A (alarm 20, overload 21.7), T200 30.4 %
1.3.envn: Nothing leaves the closed system; no oil in the field reported
1.3.eqn: A runs smoothly, vibration 1.8 mm/s; casings at 60 / 60 °C
1.3.prodn: The cat cracker draws 14.0 L/s from D-150 but gets 11.22 L/s: D-150 falls 0.56 %/min; the feed is 11 °C hotter. At the page’s training prices the station costs ≈ USD 593/h more than at design (mostly feed shortfall)
1.3.v: Time-critical for production — act within the hour
1.3.ttl: LI-150 LO (30 %) in about 11 min; the cat cracker must cut its charge before D-150 runs low

1.4.why: Nothing approaches an alarm on the pumps or a trip; stopping A would lose all the feed. The cat cracker can cut its charge if D-150 gets low.
1.4.park: Ask the cat cracker to be ready to cut its charge to about 11 L/s. Stop line: LI-150 below 30 %, TI-110 above 165 °C, TI-212 above 85 °C or II-210 above 20 A → cat cracker cuts charge, call the supervisor.

1.5.sp: A stable, reduced condition that stops the problem growing while you investigate — here the cat cracker matching its charge to what arrives, so D-150 stops falling.
1.5.tc: A consequence (safety, environment, equipment, lost production) arrives before the diagnosis is finished unless you act now.

1.6.p: Parallel pumps: the running pump’s flow, read off its curve from two local gauges, must equal what FE-100 measures; any difference goes somewhere else between the pump and FE-100.

ppl.msg: Feed 11.2 L/s with V100 at 100 %, D-150 falling; investigating now, answer within the hour
Read PI-209, PI-210 and PI-220; look, listen and touch both pumps
Be ready to cut the charge to match the feed; report your D-150 level and feed temperature
B’s maintenance next week may need extra scope

1.7.reply: The station runs safely, but only 11.2 of 14 L/s reaches the cat cracker and D-150 is falling. We are checking the pumps in the field now and will tell you within the hour whether you need to cut charge.

2.1.u: Design: A running at 32.4 m on PI-210, idle B at 0.5 m (suction head), PI-209 0.5 m, FRC-100 14 L/s with V100 84 %, II-210 13.2 A, TI-110 150 °C.

2.5.a: with the existing pumps, valves and a repair planned with B’s maintenance
2.5.r: the cat cracker needs its full charge while B is away
2.5.t: cause found within 1 h, flow restored within the shift
2.5.sf: no trip, no cavitation, no deadheaded pump
2.5.goal: Restore 14 L/s to the cat cracker with pump A alone, FRC-100 in AUTO and V100 below 90 %, within the shift, with no trip or pump damage, for less than USD 2,000.

2.6.where: Feed from P-200A through FE-100 / V100 to E-100 and D-150
2.6.who: Board operator; the cat cracker sees its feed drum falling
2.6.why: D-150 falls and the cat cracker will have to cut charge; B, the pump that “worked”, goes to maintenance next week

3.2.n: Pump A off its own curve from the field gauges: ΔH = 27.9 − 1.8 = 26.2 m → Q = √((45.0 − 26.2)/0.066327) ≈ 16.8 L/s. FE-100 measures 11.22 L/s, so ≈ 5.6 L/s leaves the discharge side before FE-100. A makes MORE than design (II-210 up agrees), so A is not weak. Idle B’s casing reads 21.9 m — close to the header, not the 0.5 m suction head — and its shaft turns backwards: liquid flows from the header back through B.

rows.chk: Running pump: flow off the curve vs FE-100

rows.c: II-210 14.2 A above design: the pump makes more flow, not less
Hotter at the same valve: less oil really goes through E-100 (FT-100 is right)
Falling at 0.56 %/min ≈ (14.0 − 11.2) L/s out of 30 m³

3.5.tree:
TOP: less than 14 L/s at FE-100 with V100 100 % and A running
 OR — A makes less (worn, slow, reverse rotation, suction starved)
 OR — more resistance after A (V201 disc, V100 not opening, E-100)
 OR — flow leaves between A and FE-100
    OR — back through the idle leg (B’s check valve + V205/V206 open)
    OR — header drain open / leak
 OR — FT-100 under-reads (the flow is really there)
3.5.cut: Single-element cut sets except the idle-leg path: {B’s check valve not seating AND V205 open AND V206 open}.

rows.st: “B is the good pump; A is tired.”
rows.how: A’s gauge and current put it ON its curve at 16.8 L/s — more than design. The flow came back with B because then A’s leg was idle, not because B is better.

3.8.n: The only change is the line-up: B ran last week, A runs now with B idle and lined up. A fault that only shows with A running and B idle sits in what the idle B leg does — or in A itself; the field readings separate the two.

3.10.n: None — all four agree that a pump flow read off the curve that is larger than FE-100 means liquid is going somewhere else.

3.11.n: The statement names no cause and Explore found nothing that contradicts it.

4.1.ideas:
B’s check valve not seating: header back through idle B
Pump A worn (wear rings / impeller)
FT-100 under-reading
Suction restriction (S-200, V200) or low NPSH
Discharge restriction after A (V201 disc, V100)
Header drain open / leak
Motor A slow or turning backwards

rows.act: Do not swap to B as “the good pump”
rows.why: B goes to maintenance next week; it would only hide the cause

rows.act: Do not raise FRC-100 or open TV-110
Read FRC-100, pumps and preheater faceplates; do the curve estimate
Field round: PI-209/210/220, both pumps; phone the cat cracker (T-1)
rows.why: Separates A worn from back-flow through B
If back-flow through B: flow returns to 14 L/s, PI-220 to suction head

5.1.proof: T-1: PI-220 21.9 m on idle B, B’s shaft backwards 318 rpm, A ≈ 16.8 L/s vs FE-100 11.22; T-2: V205 closed → 14.00 L/s, PI-220 0.5 m
5.1.mech: B’s discharge check valve no longer seats → with V205 and V206 open, header liquid runs back through idle B to the suction header (B’s casing at 21.9 m, its impeller driven backwards) → the header pressure falls and A runs out on its curve (27.9 m, ≈ 16.8 L/s, II-210 14.2 A) → only 11.22 L/s reaches FE-100, FRC-100 opens V100 to 100 % → D-150 falls, TI-110 rises. With B running and A idle (last week) A’s check valve held, so the flow was normal.

rows.opt: Close V205 now and keep it closed (B isolated from the header) until B’s maintenance
Replace B’s discharge check valve NRV-220 during B’s maintenance next week; reopen V205 when B goes back on standby
Run B and leave A on standby
Rev C: casing pressure transmitter PIT-220 with PAH on the idle pump, and an idle-leg gauge check in the shift round

rows.step: Close V205 (B discharge) in the field; B stays out of service until repaired
Tag V205 “closed — do not start B”; B start needs the check valve repaired first
If A trips while B is isolated: open V205 only with B started (B’s check valve does not matter while B runs)
Add NRV-220 replacement to B’s maintenance work order; idle-gauge check in the shift round
Tell the cat cracker: full charge restored; feed temperature back to 150 °C

rows.act: V205 closed in the field (T-2, kept as the interim fix)
NRV-220 replaced during B’s maintenance (in the OTS: the instructor clears the malfunction), V205 reopened: B back on standby

rows.pval: ≈ 0.5 m (suction head) with V205 open again

5.7.n: None: with V205 open again and the new check valve, FRC-100 14.00 L/s, OUT 83.9 %, PI-220 0.6 m on idle B, B’s shaft still, TI-110 150.1 °C.

5.8.rule: Before blaming the running pump, read the idle pump’s gauge: an idle casing must read the suction head.

6.0.n: T-1 (idle B at 21.9 m, shaft backwards), T-2 (V205 closed → 14.00 L/s) and the repair (PI-220 back to 0.6 m with V205 open) all came out as predicted.

rows.m: PIT-220 / PIT-210 with PAH on the idle pump casing (Rev C upgrade, SIS tab)
Shift round: read the idle pump’s gauge and look at its shaft after every changeover
Check valves on the pump legs in the inspection plan (seat check at each pump overhaul)

6.1.kpi: Idle-pump casing reading after each changeover: within 1 m of PI-209

rows.i: Full 14 L/s with A alone; V100 back to 84 %, TI-110 150 °C, D-150 steady
Pump A power 6.36 kW instead of 7.12 kW
D-150 was left near 30 % (LI-150 LO 30 %): FRC-100 has to run above 14 L/s for a while to refill it — agree with the cat cracker
While V205 is closed the spare cannot take over at once; a changeover needs V205 opened after B starts

hz.dev: REVERSE flow through the idle pump
hz.cause: Idle leg’s check valve not seating, suction and discharge valves open
hz.cons: Feed short, idle pump turned backwards (start against reverse rotation)
hz.sg: PAH on the idle casing; idle-gauge check in the round

hz.dev: NO standby while V205 is closed
hz.sg: Tag on V205; changeover note in the shift log

6.3.fut: In parallel pumps the idle leg is part of the running system: if its check valve fails, the spare becomes a leak.

6.4.how: Extra cost rate at the page’s training prices: USD 593/h with the fault vs USD 0/h after closing V205 (model runs: feed shortfall, power, steam) × 24 h × 7 days until B’s maintenance (assumed) − USD 1500 check valve (assumed).

6.5.again:
Read the idle pump’s gauge and shaft before blaming the running pump.
Read the running pump’s flow off its curve and compare it with the flow meter.
Use a small, reversible isolation (one valve) to prove a path before the repair.
6.5.never:
Never call one of two identical pumps “the good one” without a test.
Never leave a failed check valve in a lined-up spare.

evidence.text: FRC-100 11.22 L/s against SP 14.0, OUT 100 %; FRC-100 LO since 00:00:01.
Last week, with B running and A idle, the flow was normal (case sheet).
No operator move and no SIS event in the log before 00:20; only FRC-100 LO.
PI-220 on idle B 21.9 m (design 0.5 m = suction head).
B stopped, shaft turning backwards ≈ 318 rpm; A runs smoothly, 1.8 mm/s, rotation matches the arrow.
A off its curve: ΔH 26.2 m → ≈ 16.8 L/s; FE-100 11.22 L/s; ≈ 5.6 L/s unaccounted.
